intro: If you have typed "public law barrister near me", you are probably facing a decision by a public body that affects you or someone close to you, and you want to know whether it can be challenged. Public law barristers deal with exactly this kind of problem, using judicial review and related routes to test how public bodies have acted. iComply can introduce you to a suitable UK barrister who will quote you directly, with the price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a public law barrister usually need
need_lead: Most people who search this way are looking for a clear view on whether a public decision can be challenged, and how to go about it in time.
needs: You have received a decision from a council, government department or other public body and believe it was made unfairly or unlawfully.
You are dealing with a community care issue, such as a care package or assessment, and want to know whether the decision can be reviewed.
You think a public body has breached your human rights and want advice on whether there is a legal route to challenge it.
You have already tried the public body's own complaints or appeal process and are unsure what to do next.
You want to understand whether judicial review is realistic in your situation, and what funding options might exist before you commit.
context_heading: Timing and the pre-action stage in public law
context: Judicial review must be brought promptly, and there are strict time limits, so it is worth getting advice early rather than waiting. Before a claim is issued, a pre-action letter is normally required, setting out the complaint to the public body and giving it a chance to respond.

Funding may be available in some cases, whether through legal aid or other arrangements, so it is worth asking about this at the outset. Barristers in England and Wales are regulated by the Bar Standards Board, and you can check the Barristers' Register to see whether someone holds a current practising certificate and is authorised to accept instructions directly from the public.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the decision or action by the public body that you want to challenge, and which body made it.
Explain when you found out about the decision, as timing matters greatly in public law.
Say whether you have already complained, appealed or sent any letter to the public body.
Mention whether the issue involves community care, human rights or another area of public law.
Note where you are based, so we can introduce you to a barrister convenient to you.
Set out whether you have a solicitor already, or whether you are looking to instruct a barrister directly.
questions: Do you think my situation is suitable for judicial review, and why?
What are the time limits that apply in my case, and how soon should action be taken?
Will a pre-action letter be needed, and who would prepare it?
Can you accept instructions directly from me, or would I need a solicitor?
What funding options might be available for a case like mine?
What would you need from me to give a view on the merits?

faqs.q: What does a public law barrister actually do?
faqs.a: Public law barristers challenge decisions of public bodies through judicial review and advise on human rights and community care. They can assess whether a decision was made lawfully and set out the options open to you.

faqs.q: How do I find a public law barrister near me?
faqs.a: You can tell iComply what you need and we will introduce you to a suitable UK barrister, who will quote you directly with the price on application. You can also check the Barristers' Register to confirm a barrister's practising certificate and whether they are authorised to accept instructions directly from the public.

faqs.q: Can I instruct a barrister directly without a solicitor?
faqs.a: Many barristers can be instructed through a solicitor in the traditional way, and those registered under the Public Access scheme can be instructed directly by members of the public for suitable matters. It is worth asking the barrister whether your matter is suitable for direct instruction.

faqs.q: Is there a deadline for challenging a public body's decision?
faqs.a: Judicial review must be brought promptly, and there are strict time limits, so advice should be sought as early as possible. A pre-action letter is normally required before a claim is issued, giving the public body a chance to respond.
